## Label sources and licences

| source | licence | snapshot | positives citing it |
|---|---|---|---|
| OSV npm export (MAL-* and GitHub advisories with CWE-506) | OSV npm export: MAL-* records CC-BY-4.0 (OpenSSF malicious-packages), GitHub advisories CC-BY-4.0 | https://osv-vulnerabilities.storage.googleapis.com/npm/all.zip, downloaded 2026-10-07T02:46Z, sha256 `5a7217769c65205b…`, 222386 records | 5091 |
| tstromberg/supplychain-attack-data | tstromberg/supplychain-attack-data, Apache-2.0 | commit `a87dcc3559ca`, 84 npm attacks | 1157 |
| Incident KB (kb/incidents) | blastradius incident KB (this repository) | 12 incidents | 56 |
| Replay incidents (test/replay) | this repository | 7 incidents | 15 |

A positive can cite several sources. The GitHub advisory database API (`/advisories?cwes=506`) is not reachable from this session (sessions are bound to their repositories); its CWE-506 advisories are taken from the OSV export, which mirrors GitHub-reviewed advisories.

**Positive rule** (labels.py): a version some source calls malicious, of a package that had at least 1 release(s) not called malicious and at least 90 days of history before its first bad release (from the packument `time` map, which npm keeps for unpublished versions). Records whose versions of a package span more than 30 days are affected ranges, not publish-time compromises, and are not used for that package. Packages with more than 10 bad versions, most still live on npm, are package-level classifications and are dropped. Whole-package malware (a range covering every version) is never a positive. Positives cited only by OSV (no attack-data, KB or replay entry) must also pass two checks against attacker-owned packages, which automated scanners (OpenSSF package analysis, Amazon Inspector, ReversingLabs) report in the same way as compromises: (1) no dependency-confusion version jump (bad major more than 5 above every earlier major, e.g. 0.x → 99.99.99); (2) when no record text describes a compromise (compromised, worm, hijack, takeover, stolen, account, maintainer, phishing, a campaign name), the package needs at least 10 clean earlier releases and npm must have removed the bad release.

**Campaigns**: supplychain-attack-data ids, merged into families when their texts name the same campaign marker; KB and replay ids; positives sharing a release are one campaign; an OSV record whose text names a campaign marker joins that family (so the 2026-03-20 CanisterWorm wave is TeamPCP); named campaigns with positives within 12 h are merged; an OSV-only positive joins the named campaign with a positive within 2 days, otherwise OSV-only positives are chained in time (gap ≤ 1 day, span ≤ 14 days; named by first date). This errs towards fewer, larger campaigns so a campaign-grouped split cannot put one wave on both sides.

**Leakage warning for training.** Most positives have no manifest because npm unpublished them; negatives almost always have one. The manifest features (marked) are therefore NaN mostly on positives, and a model would learn "manifest missing → malicious". Train the history-only variant with every manifest feature masked on all rows (the `manifestFeatures` list in the schema). Training only on rows with `manifest: true` is not viable: the training split has 15 such positives. The `manifest` and `origin` row fields must never be model inputs. **Sampling bias warning.** Negatives come from packages popular enough to sit in large lockfiles, while positives include many small packages (worm waves hit whatever their victims maintained), so weekly downloads and release counts separate the classes partly because of how the negatives were chosen, not because of the attack. The positive packages' own clean releases are in the negatives to counter this; a model should be checked within package (positives against the same packages' clean releases) and with per-year weights, since positives cluster in 2025–2026 while negatives spread over 2016–2026.

## Negatives

Every release in the positives' time range of: the dependency walk from the Acme lockfiles (0 packages ranked by how many Acme packages use them; deps.dev has no top-N listing API, and today's dependents counts would be hindsight for sampling past releases), the hammer control repos' lockfiles at their pinned commits (0 packages: microsoft/TypeScript, apache/superset frontend, mochajs/mocha, microsoft/vscode, npm/cli), and the positive packages' own other releases. Removed: every version any source lists as malicious, whole-package malware, and the Acme lockfile packages (the backtest gate's noise set). Sampled to at most 12 releases per package and calendar year by a hash of name@version (deterministic). "No advisory" means no malicious-code advisory (MAL-*, CWE-506, attack data, KB); releases with ordinary vulnerability advisories stay negatives. An unpublished release of a positive package within 7 days of one of its positives is not used as a negative (458 dropped): no source lists it, but npm removed it during the attack. Manifests the replay overlay rebuilt from advisories are not used for features (`--no-reconstructed`): advisories rarely state publisher, maintainers, scripts or dependencies, so those fields would be guesses (nx 21.5.0's rebuilt manifest lacks the real postinstall hook). Those releases are described like any other unpublished release.

## Rebuild

```
cd blastradius/pack/model
curl -o osv-npm.zip https://osv-vulnerabilities.storage.googleapis.com/npm/all.zip   # check sha256 in manifest/sources.json
git clone https://github.com/tstromberg/supplychain-attack-data sad && git -C sad checkout <commit in sources.json>
python labels.py names --osv-zip osv-npm.zip --attack-data sad --root ../.. --out out/labels
python fetch_packuments.py --names out/labels/candidates.txt --cache .cache/packuments
python fetch_packuments.py --names manifest/universe-negatives.txt --cache .cache/packuments   # and universe-hammer.txt
python labels.py labels --osv-zip osv-npm.zip --attack-data sad --root ../.. --cache .cache/packuments --out out/labels
python build_dataset.py --root ../.. --cache .cache/packuments --labels out/labels --negatives manifest/universe-negatives.txt --negatives manifest/universe-hammer.txt --controls manifest/universe-controls.txt --out out/dataset --requests-only
python fetch_downloads.py --requests out/dataset/requests.jsonl --out .cache/downloads
python build_dataset.py ... --downloads .cache/downloads   # same flags, without --requests-only
python dataset_report.py --labels out/labels --dataset out/dataset --universe out/universe --sources out/sources.json --manifest manifest --report reports/<date>-dataset.md
```
